For each observation, the participant id (Id), time of day (timeofday), measurement day (day), and measurement site (site), and contextual classifications are available: environment (environment), activity context (act_context), light context (work_light_context), and photoperiod (photoperiod.state).

title: Comparison of placement error based on context
text:
This document describes a statistical analysis to investigate whether contextual factors significantly affect the differences between light measurements at the reference eye-level and on the body (chest and wrist), referred to as the placement error.
The dosimeter measurements were collected at multiple sites as part of the MeLiDos project, following the protocol of Guidolin et al. (Guidolin et al. 2024). The dataset of each site is available on GitHub:

BAUA, Dortmund, Germany (Broszio et al. 2025)
FUSPCEU, Madrid, Spain (Baeza Moyano et al. 2025)
IZTECH, Izmir, Turkey (Didikoglu et al. 2025)
KNUST, Kumasi, Ghana (Akuffo et al. 2025)
MPI, Tübingen, Germany (Guidolin et al. 2025)1
RISE, Borås, Sweden (Nilsson Tengelin et al. 2026)
THUAS, the Hague, the Netherlands (Aerts et al. 2025)
TUM, Munich, Germany (Hilden et al. 2025)
UCR, San Pedro, San José, Costa Rica (Sancho-Salas et al. 2026)

The datasets were previously prepared (see context_preparation). The resulting dataset consists of placement errors (log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements (logdif_x = log10(MEDI_x + 0.1) − log10(MEDI_h + 0.1), where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter)). For each observation, the participant id (Id), time of day (timeofday), measurement day (day), and measurement site (site), and contextual classifications are available: environment (environment), activity context (act_context), light context (work_light_context), and photoperiod (photoperiod.state).

title: Comparison of placement error based on context
text:
Research questions
Main research question: Are mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn (chest or wrist) dosimeter measurements systematically dependent on the measurement context?
Subquestion 1 (comparative): Do mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ across contexts?

Null hypothesis: For each pairwise comparison of context-specific mean log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements, the two means are equal.
Rationale: If the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements do not differ across contexts, the mean deviations can be considered context-invariant, and contextual information does not need to be considered when interpreting body-worn measurements.

Subquestion 2 (absolute): Under which contexts do the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ significantly from zero?

Null hypothesis: For each context, the mean log‑transformed difference between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements is zero.
Rationale: If the results from subquestion 1 indicate that the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements depend on context, it becomes relevant to characterize the mean deviation under each context. Testing context-specific means against zero, i.e. the value corresponding to identical measurements at both dosimeter positions, allows identifying under which contexts body-worn dosimeters exhibit systematic deviations and assessing the direction and size of those deviations.

title: Comparison of placement error based on context
text:
Model development
The following modeling decisions were made.

The dataset includes four contextual classifications describing the measurement context: activity context (act_context), light context when working indoors (work_light_context), photoperiod (photoperiod.state), and environment (environment). As measurement deviations between dosimeter positions are primarily driven by the lighting conditions and participant posture under which the measurements were performed (Vries et al. 2026a, 2026b), considerable overlap exists between these categories. For example, being outdoors typically makes daylight the most prevalent light source. Whether a participant was outdoors can be inferred from activity context, light context, and environment. Hence, to avoid multicollinearity, these contextual factors were not implemented in a single model, but a separate model was made for each factor. Each model and their rationale are described below.
The placement error (log‑transformed differences between eye‑level and body‑worn dosimeter measurements) for chest-worn (logdif_c) and wrist-worn (logdif_w) dosimeters was defined as the outcome variable for each model. The distributions of these errors show a sharp central peak and long tails, indicating leptokurtosis (kurtosis test substantially exceeded 3 for both distributions). Initial tests using a standard linear mixed-effects model (LMM), which assumes Gaussian residuals, revealed violations of the model assumptions, as evidenced by a clear S-shaped pattern in QQ plots and heteroscedasticity in residual diagnostics. Therefore, it was decided to adopt a Student-t residual distribution, as it better accommodates heavy-tailed residuals. Model diagnostics of the developed models are discussed in Section 4.
As the measurements were recorded simultaneously at the eyes, chest, and wrist, the placement errors for the chest and wrist share the same eye-level term by construction. As they are hence not fully independent, modeling both jointly was explored, but resulted in convergence errors due to the additional model complexity. Moreover, as the dependence between both errors (outcomes) is deemed outside the current scope, a separate model was fitted for each.
The dataset has a nested structure, as hourly (i.e. averaged to hourly) measurements were collected over multiple days for each participant, and each participant participated at only one site. Consequently, observations are not independent, and measurements taken on the same day, by the same participant, or at the same site were expected to be correlated. To account for these correlations, a hierarchical mixed-effects modeling framework with random effects was specified. Random intercepts were included for site, participant within site, and day within participant. Random slopes were not included, as the primary aim was to estimate population‑level context effects rather than individual‑specific differences in context responses. Although some of these nested effects explained little variance in some of the models, all were retained because their inclusion is justified on theoretical grounds based on the measurement protocol’s design.
Additionally, hourly measurements within a participant may not be independent, as an observation is expected to be correlated with the observation of the preceding hour (temporal autocorrelation). Thus, each model was checked for residual temporal autocorrelation by inspecting the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the residuals against lag. As substantial lag 1 autocorrelation was observed for all models, an AR(1) correlation structure was implemented for each participant. After implementing this structure, near-zero residual autocorrelation was observed.
Four models were developed to investigate how different contextual classifications impact placement errors. The contextual classifications were defined as fixed effects or smooths, as the aim was to estimate and compare placement errors under these specific, predefined contexts rather than to generalize to a broader population of contexts. The models (and their rationale) are:

Environment * photoperiod model (m1)
The environment * photoperiod model was built using environment (indoor or outdoor) and photoperiod.state (day or night) as contextual classifications. The other_env variable was excluded from the environment classification, as it consists of observations with both indoor and outdoor measurements, or with missing contextual data. An interaction between environment and photoperiod.state was also included, as the effect of environment on measurement deviations was expected to differ across photoperiods. The following model formula was defined:
logdif_x ~ environment * photoperiod.state + (1 | site / Id / day)
where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.
Environment * time-of-day model (m2)
The environment * time-of-day model was built using environment (indoor or outdoor) and timeofday (hourly, in local time) as contextual classifications. timeofday was anticipated to be a coarse proxy for a range of underlying contextual factors (e.g. behavioral patterns and daylight availability). It was modeled as a smooth and an interaction between both contextual classifications was included. The following model formula was defined:
logdif_x ~ environment * timeofday + (1 | site / Id / day)
where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.
Activity * photoperiod model (m3)
The activity * photoperiod model was built using act_context (home, working_indoor, road_vehicle, or outdoor_act) and photoperiod.state (day or night) as contextual classifications. The act_context factor can be seen as a more detailed description of the environmental context (compared to model m1), as whether a participant was indoors or outdoors can still be inferred from this factor. Observations with other_act were not included (as this variable represents a combination of undefined or miscellaneous activities) and an interaction between both contextual classifications was included. The formula for the model was defined as:
logdif_x ~ act_context * photoperiod.state + (1 | site / Id / day)
where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.
Indoor work lighting model (m4)
In previous work, the impact of generalized indoor (office) lighting conditions (electric ceiling-based lighting and daylighting from a vertical window or lighting from a screen) on the differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeters was simulated (Vries et al. 2026a, 2026b). Building on this, an indoor work lighting model was developed to investigate whether similar effects are present in the current real-world datasets. This was done by filtering for measurements recorded while participants reported to be working indoors, and subsequently comparing conditions based on the primary light source: 1) electric lighting, 2) daylighting, or 3) display lighting (work_light_context). A model that further subdivided categories based on the secondary light source was also considered; however, this was not continued due to the limited number of observations available.
photoperiod was not specified in this model, as the occurrence of “daylight” as a light source inherently explains the photoperiod. The formula for the model was defined as:
logdif_x ~ work_light_context + (1 | site / Id / day)
where x refers to either the chest (c) or wrist (w) dosimeter.



Several modeling frameworks were considered to accommodate the nested structure of the data through random effects and the heavy‑tailed distributions of logdif_c and logdif_w through a Student-t residual distribution. Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were considered; however, the implementation of a Student‑t residual distribution is not straightforward, as this distribution does not belong to the exponential family typically underlying GLMMs. Bayesian hierarchical models were also considered, as they naturally allow the specification of heavy-tailed distributions. However, a frequentist framework was preferred to retain direct test statistics and p-values for reporting, and because more resources were available to support model development. Therefore, a generalized additive model (GAM) framework (with random effects) was adopted. Although all fixed effects in the models m1, m3, and m4 are categorical, implying a linear mean structure, the GAM framework supports Student‑t residual distributions while retaining a mixed‑effects formulation. Hence, for these models, the GAM was not used to model nonlinear predictor effects, but rather as a general framework for mixed-effects modeling with heavy-tailed residuals.

title: Comparison of placement error based on context
text:
Fit and evaluate models
Models were fitted using the mgcv package. Random effects were implemented using bs = “re”. Because mgcv does not use the lme4-style formula syntax (i.e. site / Id / day), the structure was specified using grouping factors rather than nesting operators. Each participant was observed at only one site, having a unique ID, so the participant’s random effect was implicitly nested within site by design. Measurement day was not unique across participants, and therefore day‑within‑participant was represented by a constructed grouping factor that explicitly nested days within participants.

#| label: format-random-effects

# Create a nested category for Id/day
m1m2_data$Id_day <- interaction(m1m2_data$Id, m1m2_data$day, drop = TRUE)
m3_data$Id_day <- interaction(m3_data$Id, m3_data$day, drop = TRUE)
m4_data$Id_day <- interaction(m4_data$Id, m4_data$day, drop = TRUE)

# Convert Id to factor
m1m2_data$Id <- factor(m1m2_data$Id)
m3_data$Id <- factor(m3_data$Id)
m4_data$Id <- factor(m4_data$Id)

# Count the number of participants and participant-days for each model
tibble(
  dataset = c("Environment * photoperiod model (m1), Environment * time-of-day model (m2)", "Activity * photoperiod model (m3)", "Indoor work lighting model (m4)"),
  participants = c(n_distinct(m1m2_data$Id),
                       n_distinct(m3_data$Id),
                       n_distinct(m4_data$Id)),
  participant_days = c(n_distinct(m1m2_data$Id_day),
                       n_distinct(m3_data$Id_day),
                       n_distinct(m4_data$Id_day))
) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "dataset") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(participants, participant_days),
             decimals = 0, sep_mark = ",") |>
  cols_label(
    participants     = "Participants",
    participant_days = "Participant-days"
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = list(cells_stub(), cells_column_labels())
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Participants and participant-days per model"
  )

Models were fitted using the bam() function with the fast restricted maximum likelihood (fREML) method and the discrete = TRUE option. This was preferred over gam() with standard REML because the latter resulted in substantially longer computation times given the dataset size (approximately 10,000 observations). Comparisons against both gam() with REML and bam() with discrete = FALSE showed that fixed-effect estimates agreed to three decimal places in each case (maximum absolute difference < 0.001 log₁₀ units), confirming no meaningful impact on these model predictions.

Environment * photoperiod model (m1)

m1_logdif_c <- bam(

Environment * time-of-day model (m2)

Investigation on time of day smooth modeling approach
An average time of day smooth and separate smooths for each environment are defined. If the standard second derivative penalty (m=2) is applied to the average and by environment smooths, the two functions may look very similar, which could result in the model not being able to attribute structure to one versus the other (resulting in very large confidence intervals). This can be prevented by specifying m=1 for the by environment smooths, so that the penalty acts on the first derivative, and thus the by environment smooth measures deviations from the average smooth. However, this fix is only valid for TPRS and B-splines, and may induce piecewise linear behavior.
To investigate how the time of day smooths should be implemented, six different modeling approaches are compared. The first three treat the smooth as non-cyclic, the latter three as cyclic.

#| label: temp-model-investigation

# Fit models without AR
# Non-cyclic models
mA_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, m = 1, k = 12) +
    s(timeofday, k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML"
)

mB_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, m = 2, k = 12) +
    s(timeofday, k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML"
)

mC_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ 
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, k = 12) +
    s(timeofday, environment, bs = "sz", k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML"
)

# Cyclic models
mD_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, bs = "cc", k = 12, m = 1) +
    s(timeofday, bs = "cc", k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML",
  knots = list(timeofday = c(0, 24))
)

mE_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, bs = "cc", k = 12, m = 2) +
    s(timeofday, bs = "cc", k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML",
  knots = list(timeofday = c(0, 24))
)

mF_init <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ 
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, bs = "cc", k = 12) +
    s(timeofday, environment, bs = "sz", k = 12, xt = list(bs = "cc")),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML",
  knots = list(timeofday = c(0, 24))
)

rho_A <- start_value_rho(mA_init)
rho_B <- start_value_rho(mB_init)
rho_C <- start_value_rho(mC_init)
rho_D <- start_value_rho(mD_init)
rho_E <- start_value_rho(mE_init)
rho_F <- start_value_rho(mF_init)


# Fit models with AR
mA <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, m = 1, k = 12) + # One time of day smooth for each environment
    s(timeofday, k = 12), # Average smooth effect of time of day
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML",
  rho = rho_A, AR.start = AR.start
)

mB <- bam(
  logdif_c ~ environment +
    s(site, bs = "re") + s(Id, bs = "re") + s(Id_day, bs = "re") +
    s(timeofday, by = environment, m = 2, k = 12) +
    s(timeofday, k = 12),
  data = m1m2_data, family = scat(),
  discrete = TRUE, nthreads = 10, method = "fREML",
  rho = rho_B, AR.start = AR.start
)

# Sz basis allows us to do a factor by smooth without changing to a first derivative
# penalty (m=1). So basically all advantages of the factor by model, but not the possible limitations.

# Plot model predictions
backtrans_pct <- function(x) (10^x - 1) * 100

get_curve <- function(model, data, label, 
                      times = seq(0, 24, by = 0.25)) {
  pred_grid <- expand.grid(
    environment = c("indoor", "outdoor"),
    timeofday   = times,
    site        = data$site[1],
    Id          = data$Id[1],
    Id_day      = data$Id_day[1],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  Xp <- predict(
    model, newdata = pred_grid,
    exclude = c("s(site)", "s(Id)", "s(Id_day)"),
    type    = "lpmatrix"
  )
  
  beta  <- coef(model)
  Vbeta <- vcov(model)
  fit   <- as.numeric(Xp %*% beta)
  se    <- sqrt(rowSums((Xp %*% Vbeta) * Xp))
  
  pred_grid |>
    mutate(
      pct_error      = backtrans_pct(fit),
      pct_error_low  = backtrans_pct(fit - 1.96 * se),
      pct_error_high = backtrans_pct(fit + 1.96 * se),
      model          = label
    )
}

curves_all <- bind_rows(
  Map(get_curve, models, list(m1m2_data), labels)
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = labels))

The cyclic models outperformed the non-cyclic ones on AIC and R2. A cyclic specification is also more appropriate on theoretical grounds, since placement errors just before and after midnight should roughly align. On visual inspection, the predictions for the cyclic models (D, E, and F) were approximately identical. Models D and E were identical in AIC and R2, and outperformed model F. Because model D applies the m=1 fix, which is not valid for the cyclic (cc) basis (but was kept in for consistency with the non-cyclic models), it behaves identically to model E (which uses the standard m=2 penalty). Since E outperforms F and the wide confidence interval problem that the m=1 fix is meant to address does not appear present for the m=2 specification, the time-of-day smooth was implemented as in model E.

All models converged with ν = 3, the lower bound of the scat() family. This indicates that the residuals are at least as heavy-tailed as a t₃ distribution; the true residual distribution may be heavier still, but cannot be represented within this family. No alternative family available in mgcv accommodates heavier-tailed distributions, so this is a limitation of the modeling approach, which in turn results in limitations in the model diagnostics (discussed later). The scale parameter σ is consistently larger for the wrist models than for the chest models, indicating greater residual spread for wrist-versus-eye-level differences after accounting for fixed effects, smooths, and random effects.
Wrist R² consistently exceeds chest R², meaning the model explains more variance for wrist deviations than for chest deviations. Combined with the larger σ for wrist, this implies that wrist deviations are both larger in absolute terms and better predicted by the fixed effects. Overall, however, deviance explained (and R²) is low across all models. This is expected as the outcome is a difference between two noisy paired measurements, which removes the variance shared between dosimeter positions and isolates position-specific noise; and the contextual factors are coarse categorical contrasts that cannot capture within-category variation in actual lighting conditions. Hence, these values are deemed acceptable as the aim of the models is to test whether systematic mean deviations exist across contexts, not to maximize predictive performance.
For all chest models, the site random effect did not contribute meaningfully, but was retained for consistency across models.

  y_label = "Response", 
  title = "Observed vs fitted values")








Across all eight models, the central body of the residual distribution closely follows the reference line, indicating that the mean structure of the model is adequate. The lower tail consistently sits below the reference line, indicating that the residuals are more negative than the fitted scaled-t (ν = 3) distribution predicts. The upper tail is closer to the reference line, with generally modest deviations. The optimizer pushed the residual distribution toward the heaviest tails available, but this is still not heavy enough to accommodate the most extreme negative residuals. Overall, the chest models appear less well matched than the wrist models.
These diagnostics are not optimal. However, the outcome variable has already been transformed to improve model fit and cannot reasonably be transformed further. This is an inherent difficulty of modeling errors of this kind. Model fit is therefore taken into account when interpreting the results, by focusing on the mean values and remaining conservative in the interpretation.

title: Comparison of placement error based on context
text:
Placement errors between contexts (comparative)
Subquestion 1 was formulated as: “Do mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ across contexts?”
Using the fitted models and the emmeans package, estimated marginal means of the log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements were computed for each combination of contextual predictors. To identify if there are significant differences between the marginal means under each context, all combinations were compared using model-based t-tests (targeted contrasts). Confidence intervals and p-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, as in this analysis a false negative carries greater consequence than a false positive.

Results table

#| label: calculate-emmeans

# Compute the estimated marginal means for each combination
# Each factor that is in the model is also in the emmeans calculation, thus no weighting needed
emm_logdif_c_m1 <- emmeans(m1_logdif_c, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w_m1 <- emmeans(m1_logdif_w, ~ environment * photoperiod.state)

emm_logdif_c_m3 <- emmeans(m3_logdif_c, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)
emm_logdif_w_m3 <- emmeans(m3_logdif_w, ~ act_context * photoperiod.state)

emm_logdif_c_m4 <- emmeans(m4_logdif_c, ~ work_light_context)
emm_logdif_w_m4 <- emmeans(m4_logdif_w, ~ work_light_context)

# Marginal means for time of day are calculated in 6 hour bins
emm_logdif_c_m2 <- emmeans(m2_logdif_c, ~ environment | timeofday, at = list(timeofday = seq(0, 18, by = 6)))
emm_logdif_w_m2 <- emmeans(m2_logdif_w, ~ environment | timeofday, at = list(timeofday = seq(0, 18, by = 6)))


# Build dataset with emmean contrasts
build_block <- function(emm_obj, position, source, by_var = NULL) {
  emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm_obj)

  # Exclude the stratifier (if any) plus the standard stat columns
  ctx_col <- setdiff(names(emm_df),
                     c(by_var, "emmean", "SE", "df", "lower.CL", "upper.CL"))

  emm_small <- emm_df |>
    select(all_of(by_var), all_of(ctx_col), emmean) |>
    rename(context_level = !!ctx_col)

  # Contrast: stratified by by_var when supplied, unstratified otherwise
  ct <- contrast(emm_obj, method = "pairwise", by = by_var, adjust = "none")

  # Join keys: include by_var only when stratifying
  join_a <- c(by_var, c("ctx_a_raw" = "context_level"))
  join_b <- c(by_var, c("ctx_b_raw" = "context_level"))

  as.data.frame(summary(ct)) |>
    mutate(
      ctx_a_raw = str_split_fixed(contrast, " - ", 2)[, 1],
      ctx_b_raw = str_split_fixed(contrast, " - ", 2)[, 2]
    ) |>
    left_join(emm_small, by = join_a) |>
    rename(emm_a = emmean) |>
    left_join(emm_small, by = join_b) |>
    rename(emm_b = emmean) |>
    mutate(position = position, source = source)
}

blocks <- bind_rows(
  build_block(emm_logdif_c_m1, "Chest", "m1", by_var = "photoperiod.state"),
  build_block(emm_logdif_w_m1, "Wrist", "m1", by_var = "photoperiod.state"),
  build_block(emm_logdif_c_m3, "Chest", "m3", by_var = "photoperiod.state"),
  build_block(emm_logdif_w_m3, "Wrist", "m3", by_var = "photoperiod.state"),
  build_block(emm_logdif_c_m4, "Chest", "m4"),
  build_block(emm_logdif_w_m4, "Wrist", "m4")
)

format_blocks <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      position = factor(position, levels = c("Chest", "Wrist")),
      # photoperiod is NA for m4 rows; that's expected and unused by the m4 outputs
      photoperiod = factor(photoperiod.state,
                           levels = c("day", "night"),
                           labels = c("Day", "Night")),
      # table display strings
      ctxA = label_term(ctx_a_raw),
      ctxB = label_term(ctx_b_raw),
      logdifA = sprintf("%.3f", emm_a),
      logdifB = sprintf("%.3f", emm_b),
      ratioA = sprintf("%.3f", 10^emm_a),
      ratioB = sprintf("%.3f", 10^emm_b),
      errA = sprintf("%+.1f", (10^emm_a - 1) * 100),
      errB = sprintf("%+.1f", (10^emm_b - 1) * 100),
      delta = sprintf("%.3f", estimate),
      fold = sprintf("%.2f", 10^estimate),
      pval = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value)),
      pval_num = p.value,
      # plot fields
      cell_label = sprintf("%.2f\u00d7", 10^estimate),   # fold-change
      is_sig = p.value < 0.05
    )
}

fmt <- format_blocks(blocks)


#| label: overview-table-contrasts

# Plot the results for model m1, m3, and m4. As model m2 is time based, it is not included in this table
contrast_levels_m1m3 <- c(
  "indoor - outdoor",
  "home - working_indoor",
  "home - road_vehicle",
  "home - outdoor_act",
  "working_indoor - road_vehicle",
  "working_indoor - outdoor_act",
  "road_vehicle - outdoor_act"
)

contrast_levels_m4 <- c(
  "electric - daylight",
  "electric - display",
  "daylight - display"
)

# Pretty contrast labeller (raw "a - b" -> "Label A − Label B")
nice_contrast <- function(raw) {
  vapply(raw, function(s) {
    p <- strsplit(s, " - ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    paste(label_term(p[1]), label_term(p[2]), sep = " \u2212 ")
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

# Define the columns for each table
# 12 sub-columns per (position, photoperiod) block, in display order.
# pval_num is carried to make significant p values bold

sub_cols <- c("ctxA", "logdifA", "ratioA", "errA",
              "ctxB", "logdifB", "ratioB", "errB",
              "delta", "fold", "pval", "pval_num")

# Pivot a formatted subset to wide. periods = NULL means no split for day or night (m4).
to_wide <- function(df, contrast_levels, periods = c("Day", "Night")) {
  d <- df |>
    filter(contrast %in% contrast_levels) |>
    mutate(contrast = factor(contrast, levels = contrast_levels)) |>
    arrange(contrast)

  if (is.null(periods)) {
    w <- d |>
      select(contrast, position, all_of(sub_cols)) |>
      pivot_wider(names_from = position,
                  values_from = all_of(sub_cols),
                  names_glue = "{position}_{.value}")
    ordered <- c("contrast",
      unlist(lapply(c("Chest", "Wrist"),
                    \(pos) paste(pos, sub_cols, sep = "_"))))
  } else {
    w <- d |>
      select(contrast, position, photoperiod, all_of(sub_cols)) |>
      pivot_wider(names_from = c(position, photoperiod),
                  values_from = all_of(sub_cols),
                  names_glue = "{position}_{photoperiod}_{.value}")
    ordered <- c("contrast",
      unlist(lapply(c("Chest", "Wrist"), \(pos)
        unlist(lapply(periods, \(per) paste(pos, per, sub_cols, sep = "_"))))))
  }

  w <- w[, ordered]
  # relabel contrasts
  w |>
    mutate(contrast = factor(contrast,
                             levels = contrast_levels,
                             labels = nice_contrast(contrast_levels)))
}

wide_tbl_m1m3 <- to_wide(fmt, contrast_levels_m1m3, periods = c("Day", "Night"))
wide_tbl_m4 <- to_wide(fmt, contrast_levels_m4, periods = NULL)

# Table m1m3
make_spanners_m1m3 <- function(g) {
  for (pos in c("Chest", "Wrist")) {
    for (per in c("Day", "Night")) {
      cols_A <- paste(pos, per, c("ctxA", "logdifA", "ratioA", "errA"),
                        sep = "_")
      cols_B <- paste(pos, per, c("ctxB", "logdifB", "ratioB", "errB"),
                        sep = "_")
      cols_cmp <- paste(pos, per, c("delta", "fold", "pval", "pval_num"),
                        sep = "_")

      g <- g |>
        tab_spanner(label = "Context A", columns = all_of(cols_A),
                    id = paste0(pos, "_", per, "_A")) |>
        tab_spanner(label = "Context B", columns = all_of(cols_B),
                    id = paste0(pos, "_", per, "_B")) |>
        tab_spanner(label = "Contrast comparison", columns = all_of(cols_cmp),
                    id = paste0(pos, "_", per, "_cmp"))

      cols_per <- paste(pos, per, sub_cols, sep = "_")
      g <- g |>
        tab_spanner(label = per, columns = all_of(cols_per),
                    id = paste0(pos, "_", per), level = 2)
    }
    pos_cols <- paste(pos,
                      rep(c("Day", "Night"), each = length(sub_cols)),
                      rep(sub_cols, 2),
                      sep = "_")
    g <- g |> tab_spanner(label = pos, columns = all_of(pos_cols),
                          id = pos, level = 3)
  }
  g
}

text:
Placement error per context (absolute)
Subquestion 2 was formulated as: “Under which contexts do the mean log-transformed differences between eye-level and body-worn dosimeter measurements differ significantly from zero?”
Each estimated marginal mean was tested against zero using model‑based t‑tests, where a value of zero corresponds to the eye-level and body-worn dosimeters measuring the same value. A negative estimate indicates that eye-level measurements were higher than body-worn measurements. For interpretability, estimates were back-transformed to percentage errors. Confidence intervals and p-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, as in this analysis a false negative carries greater consequence than a false positive.

# Create a table for each model

get_emm_table <- function(emm_obj) {
  emm_test <- as.data.frame(test(emm_obj, null = 0, adjust = "none"))
  emm_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(emm_obj, level = 0.95, adjust = "none"))
  emm_test |>
    mutate(lower.CL = emm_ci$lower.CL,
           upper.CL = emm_ci$upper.CL)
}

# Combine chest + wrist EMMs, convert log10 differences to % error, relabel outcome
build_pct_table <- function(emm_c_obj, emm_w_obj) {
  bind_rows(
    get_emm_table(emm_c_obj) |> mutate(outcome = "Chest-worn dosimeter"),
    get_emm_table(emm_w_obj) |> mutate(outcome = "Wrist-worn dosimeter")
  ) |>
    mutate(
      pct_error = 100 * (10^emmean - 1),
      pct_error_low = 100 * (10^lower.CL - 1),
      pct_error_high = 100 * (10^upper.CL - 1)
    )
}

# Shared gt styling
style_pct_gt <- function(df, label_map, title) {
  df |>
    gt(groupname_col = "outcome") |>
    cols_label(.list = label_map) |>
    tab_spanner(label = "95% CI",
                columns = c(pct_error_low, pct_error_high)) |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(pct_error, pct_error_low, pct_error_high),
               decimals = 1) |>
    fmt(columns = p.value,
        fns = function(x) ifelse(x < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", x))) |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
              locations = cells_body(columns = p.value,
                                     rows = p.value < 0.05)) |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
              locations = list(cells_row_groups(),
                               cells_column_labels())) |>
    tab_header(title = title)
}

backtrans_pct <- function(x) (10^x - 1) * 100

# Prepare data
prep_df <- function(emm_obj, group_var, position_label) {
  df <- get_emm_table(emm_obj)
  df$category <- df[[group_var]]
  df$position <- position_label
  df |>
    select(category, photoperiod.state, emmean, lower.CL, upper.CL, p.value, position) |>
    mutate(
      pct_est = backtrans_pct(emmean),
      pct_lower = backtrans_pct(lower.CL),
      pct_upper = backtrans_pct(upper.CL),
      is_sig = p.value < 0.05,
      period = factor(photoperiod.state, levels = c("day", "night"),
                      labels = c("Day", "Night")),
      line_color = photoperiod_colors[as.character(photoperiod.state)],
      point_fill = ifelse(is_sig, line_color, "white")
    )
}

prep_df_m4 <- function(emm_obj, position_label) {
  df <- get_emm_table(emm_obj)
  df$category <- df$work_light_context
  df$position <- position_label
  df |>
    select(category, emmean, lower.CL, upper.CL, p.value, position) |>
    mutate(
      pct_est = backtrans_pct(emmean),
      pct_lower = backtrans_pct(lower.CL),
      pct_upper = backtrans_pct(upper.CL),
      is_sig = p.value < 0.05,
      line_color = pos_colors[tolower(position_label)],
      point_fill = ifelse(is_sig, line_color, "white")
    )
}

p_m3 <- ggplot(df_m3, aes(x = pct_est, y = category)) +
  gridlines +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = pct_lower, xmax = pct_upper,
                     color = period, group = period),
                 position = pd, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(color = period, fill = point_fill, group = period),
             shape = 21, position = pd, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Day = unname(photoperiod_colors["day"]),
               Night = unname(photoperiod_colors["night"])),
    name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  facet_wrap2(~ position) +
  x_scale +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Activity") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(color = NA),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        plot.margin = margin(t = 0, r = 5, b = 0, l = 5)) +
  hidden_x

# p_m4: strips (chest/wrist) hidden, x shown, no legend
p_m4 <- ggplot(df_m4, aes(x = pct_est, y = category)) +
  gridlines +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = pct_lower, xmax = pct_upper, color = line_color),
                 linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(color = line_color, fill = point_fill),
             shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  facet_wrap2(~ position) +
  x_scale +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) +
  labs(x = "Error (%)", y = "Indoor work lighting\u00b3") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(color = NA),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 0, r = 5, b = 0, l = 5))

# p_m2: time of day curves, colored strips (chest/wrist), x shown, legend
get_emm_curve <- function(model, position_label) {
  emm <- emmeans(model, ~ environment | timeofday,
                 at = list(timeofday = seq(0, 24, by = 0.25)))
  emm_test <- as.data.frame(test(emm, null = 0, adjust = "none"))
  emm_ci   <- as.data.frame(confint(emm, level = 0.95, adjust = "none"))
  emm_test |>
    mutate(lower.CL = emm_ci$lower.CL,
           upper.CL = emm_ci$upper.CL,
           pct_error = backtrans_pct(emmean),
           pct_error_low = backtrans_pct(lower.CL),
           pct_error_high = backtrans_pct(upper.CL),
           significant = p.value < 0.05,
           position = position_label)
}

curves <- bind_rows(get_emm_curve(m2_logdif_c, "Chest"),
                    get_emm_curve(m2_logdif_w, "Wrist")) |>
  arrange(position, environment, timeofday) |>
  mutate(position    = factor(position, levels = c("Chest", "Wrist")),
         environment = factor(environment, levels = c("indoor", "outdoor"))) |>
  mutate(signif_id = consecutive_id(significant),
         .by = c(position, environment))

y_data_range  <- range(c(curves$pct_error_low, curves$pct_error_high), na.rm = TRUE)
y_grid_breaks <- seq(floor(y_data_range[1] / 10) * 10,
                     ceiling(y_data_range[2] / 10) * 10, by = 10)
y_grid_breaks <- y_grid_breaks[y_grid_breaks != 0]

p_m2 <- ggplot(curves, aes(x = timeofday, y = pct_error, color = environment)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pct_error_low, ymax = pct_error_high, fill = environment),
              alpha = 0.20, color = NA) +
  map(y_grid_breaks,
      \(yv) geom_hline(yintercept = yv, linewidth = 0.5,
                       color = "grey70", linetype = "dotted")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = "Non-signif.")) +
  geom_line(data = curves |> filter(significant),
            aes(group = interaction(environment, signif_id),
                linewidth = "Significant")) +
  facet_wrap2(~ position, strip = strip_pos) +
  scale_color_manual(values = env_colors,
                     labels = c(indoor = "Indoors", outdoor = "Outdoors"),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = env_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c("Significant" = 1.4, "Non-signif." = 0.5),
    limits = c("Significant", "Non-signif."),
    name = NULL,
    guide = guide_legend(order = 2,
                         override.aes = list(colour = "black", fill = NA))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(y) paste0(ifelse(y > 0, "+", ""), y, "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 24)) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(order = 1,
                              override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.4))) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  labs(x = "Local time (hrs)", y = "Error (%)", tag = "B") +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))

# Combine plots
top <- (p_m1 / plot_spacer() / p_m3 / plot_spacer() / p_m4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(2, -1.3, 4, -1.3, 3))

final_plot <- wrap_plots(top, plot_spacer(), p_m2,
                         ncol = 1, heights = c(7.8, 0, 3.8)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Placement error (% melEDI) by context",
    subtitle = "Mean placement errors (melEDI) and 95% confidence intervals (horizontal lines or shaded bands).\nEstimates significantly different from zero (p < 0.05) are shown as filled circles or bold curves.",
    caption = paste(
      "\u00b9 Environment: Inside (indoors) or outside (outdoors) a building",
      "\u00b2 Cycling/walking, working, or leisure outdoors",
      "\u00b3 Primary light source when working in the office/home",
      sep = "<br>"),
    theme = theme(plot.caption = element_markdown(hjust = 0, size = 8)))

final_plot

ggsave(here("output/figures/absolute_context_error.pdf"),
       plot   = final_plot,
       width  = 8,
       height = 9,
       units  = "in")

ggsave(here("output/figures/absolute_context_error.jpeg"),
       plot   = final_plot,
       width  = 8,
       height = 9,
       units  = "in")


# Extract minimum and maximum placement error for time of day
curves |>
  group_by(position, environment) |>
  summarise(
    min_pct   = min(pct_error),
    min_time  = timeofday[which.min(pct_error)],
    max_pct   = max(pct_error),
    max_time  = timeofday[which.max(pct_error)],
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  position environment min_pct min_time max_pct max_time
  <fct>    <fct>         <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Chest    indoor        -23.6     22.2  -8.49      5.75
2 Chest    outdoor       -16.4     22.2   0.229     5.75
3 Wrist    indoor        -44.5     21.2 -23.3       5.5 
4 Wrist    outdoor       -49.8     21.2 -22.0      12.8 








Figure 2: Placement errors under each context. A negative percentage indicates that the body-worn dosimeter underestimates eye-level light exposure. Confidence intervals are asymmetric on the percentage scale because back-transformation from log space is nonlinear. Confidence intervals and p-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Setup
The following packages are loaded for data wrangling (tidyverse), mixed-effects modelling (lme4, lmerTest, glmmTMB), post-hoc contrasts (emmeans), model diagnostics (performance, car), light-logger data utilities (LightLogR, melidosData), and table/plot formatting (gt, gtsummary, ggplot2, cowplot, gghighlight, see, fontawesome, katex, ggplot2).

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(see)
library(readxl)
library(gghighlight)
library(cowplot)
library(glmmTMB)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(melidosData)
library(emmeans)
library(here)
library(car)
library(performance)
library(LightLogR)
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)
library(katex)

library(stringr)

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Import
The pre-processed metrics are loaded from a single .RData file produced by the preparation notebook. This object (metrics) is a long-format data frame with one row per participant, date, wearing position, and metric.

load(here("data/prepared_metrics.RData"))


Derive wake and sleep duration denominators
Timing differences are expressed relative to the behavioural interval in which the underlying metric is defined. The sleep interval follows the preparation workflow and extends from diary-recorded sleepprep (when the devices were positioned for the night) to wake. Diary intervals are restricted to participant-dates retained in the prepared metrics, with each interval assigned to its wake date. Mean sleep duration is the grand mean across all retained diary intervals, so each retained night receives equal weight. Mean wake duration is the complement of mean sleep duration to 24 hours. The three darkest-10-hour timing outcomes are classified as darkness-based; all other timing outcomes are classified as brightness-based.



Derive grand-mean wake and sleep durations

analysis_days <-
  metrics |>
  filter(!is.na(Date)) |>
  transmute(
    Id = as.character(Id),
    Date = as.Date(Date)
  ) |>
  distinct()

sleep_intervals <-
  load_data("sleepdiaries") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "diary_site") |>
  filter(
    !is.na(sleepprep),
    !is.na(wake)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Id = as.character(Id),
    Date = as.Date(wake),
    sleep_duration_seconds = as.numeric(
      difftime(wake, sleepprep, units = "secs")
    )
  ) |>
  semi_join(analysis_days, by = join_by(Id, Date))

invalid_sleep_intervals <-
  sleep_intervals |>
  filter(
    !is.finite(sleep_duration_seconds) |
      sleep_duration_seconds <= 0 |
      sleep_duration_seconds >= 24 * 60 * 60
  )

if (nrow(invalid_sleep_intervals) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "At least one diary-defined sleep interval is outside (0, 24) hours.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

mean_sleep_duration_seconds <- mean(sleep_intervals$sleep_duration_seconds)
mean_wake_duration_seconds <- 24 * 60 * 60 - mean_sleep_duration_seconds

format_duration <- function(seconds) {
  total_minutes <- round(seconds / 60)
  sprintf(
    "%d h %02d min",
    total_minutes %/% 60,
    total_minutes %% 60
  )
}

mean_sleep_duration_label <- format_duration(mean_sleep_duration_seconds)
mean_wake_duration_label <- format_duration(mean_wake_duration_seconds)
mean_sleep_one_percent_label <-
  sprintf("%.1f min", mean_sleep_duration_seconds / 100 / 60)
mean_wake_one_percent_label <-
  sprintf("%.1f min", mean_wake_duration_seconds / 100 / 60)

darkness_timing_metrics <- c(
  "darkest_10h_midpoint",
  "darkest_10h_onset",
  "darkest_10h_offset"
)

timing_normalization_footnote <- paste0(
  "Timing effects and timing-model SDs use the grand mean diary-defined ",
  "wake duration (", mean_wake_duration_label,
  "; 1% = ", mean_wake_one_percent_label,
  ") for brightness-based timing metrics and the grand mean diary-defined ",
  "sleep duration (", mean_sleep_duration_label,
  "; 1% = ", mean_sleep_one_percent_label,
  ") for darkness-based timing metrics. All other metrics use the absolute ",
  "glasses reference on the modelling scale."
)


The resulting grand means are 15 h 44 min of wake and 8 h 16 min of sleep. Consequently, 1% represents 9.4 min for brightness-based timing metrics and 5.0 min for darkness-based timing metrics.

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Visualizing metrics
A few shared plotting helpers are defined here: a log-scale break sequence, a named color vector (one color per wearing position), and a number formatter for axis labels.



helpers

breaks <- c(0, 10^(0:5))
colors <- ggsci::pal_jco()(3) |> set_names(c("glasses", "chest", "wrist"))
scenario_label <- "Primary analysis: documented non-wear removed; diary-defined sleep retained"
label <- function(x) format(x, 
      scientific = FALSE, big.mark = " ")

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Preparing metric table
The raw metrics data frame is restructured for per-metric modelling. Factor levels are set for position, Id, site, and Date (missing dates are replaced with a sentinel value so they don’t drop). The data are then nested so that each row in metrics_nested holds all observations for a single metric.



nest data

metrics_nested <-
  metrics |> 
  mutate(Date = replace_na(Date, as_date("2024-09-01")),
         position = factor(position, levels = c("glasses", "chest", "wrist")),
         Id = factor(Id),
         site = factor(site),
         Date = factor(Date)) |> 
  nest(data = -c(metric))


Metadata for each metric (model engine, response transformation, metric type, etc.) is read from an Excel file. The engine column determines which modelling function to use (lm, lmer, glmer, glmmTMB), and the corresponding distributional family is constructed here. The metadata is then joined onto the nested data frame so every metric row knows how it should be modelled.



Load metric information

metric_info <- read_xlsx(here("data/metric_types.xlsx"))
metric_info <- 
metric_info |> 
  mutate(family = map(engine, \(x) switch(x,
                              "lm" = gaussian(),
                              "lmer" = gaussian(),
                              "glmer" = poisson(),
                              "glmmTMB" = tweedie(link = "log"))),
         family = map2(family, note, 
                       \(x,y) ifelse(is.na(y), return(x), return(poisson()))
                       )
         ) |> 
  select(-note)





Combine metric data and metadata

metrics_nested <- 
metrics_nested |> 
  left_join(metric_info, by = join_by(metric == name))



Scaling nighttime metrics
Metrics that capture timing and might cross midnight need to be rescaled in order to work with linear models. The next plot shows the distribution of timing metrics.



show distribution of timing metrics

metrics_nested |> 
  filter(metric_type == "timing") |> 
  unnest(data) |> 
    group_by(Id, metric) |> 
  mutate(
    position = fct_relevel(position, c("chest", "glasses", "wrist")),
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=position, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(col = position), height = 0,             
              width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(col = position, fill = position), alpha = 0.5,
               width = 0.1,
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.2)) +
  geom_violinhalf(aes(x = position, y = value,
                   col = position, fill = position), 
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.3),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors) + 
  facet_wrap(~metric, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  guides(col = "none", fill = "none") +
  labs(y = "Scaled and centered metric values",
       x = "Wearing position",
       title = "Raincloud plots of scaled and centered metric results",
       subtitle = scenario_label) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  scale_y_time()








Figure 1





Affected metrics are:

darkest 10 hours midpoint
darkest 10 hours onset

Both show a clear split of the data around midnight. To resolve this, we will shift the datas so that data after 12:00 midday are negative values (i.e., indicate time before midnight).



Transform nighttime timing metrics

metrics_nested <- 
metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(data = map2(data, metric, 
                     \(data, name) {
                       if(name %in% c("darkest_10h_midpoint", "darkest_10h_onset")) {
                         data |> 
                           mutate(value = 
                                    ifelse(value >= (12*60*60), 
                                           value - 24*60*60, 
                                           value)
                                  )
                       } else data
                     }))

text:
Visualize metric distribution
To get an overview of how metrics behave across wearing positions, all metrics are scaled and centered within participant–metric groups and displayed as raincloud plots (jittered points + boxplot + half-violin). Lines connecting the same participant–date across positions reveal within-person consistency. The figure is saved as a PDF for publication.



Show distribution of all metrics

fig_metric_distribution <- metrics |>
  group_by(Id, metric) |> 
  mutate(
    position = fct_relevel(position, c("chest", "glasses", "wrist")),
    value = base::scale(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=position, y = value)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = interaction(Id, Date)), alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_jitter(aes(col = position), height = 0,             
              width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(col = position, fill = position), alpha = 0.5,
               width = 0.1,
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.2)) +

                   col = position, fill = position), 
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.3),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors) + 
  facet_wrap(~metric, ncol = 5) +
  guides(col = "none", fill = "none") +
  labs(y = "Scaled and centered metric values",
       x = "Wearing position",
       title = "Raincloud plots of scaled and centered metric results",
       subtitle = scenario_label) +
  theme_cowplot()

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Prepare modelling
The primary hypothesis (H1) is that wearing position affects a metric, potentially differently across measurement sites (i.e., a site × position interaction). The right-hand side of the formula is assembled here by appending the pre-specified random-effects structure (stored in the random column of metric_info) to the fixed-effects template ~ site*position. A helper then collects all formula column names (H0 and H1 variants) for programmatic iteration.
The table below summarises the modelling specification for every metric: the response variable, any pre-transformation applied, the modelling engine, the distributional family, and the full H1 formula. Confirmatory analyses deliberately omit p-value correction, because a non-significant position effect is the more scientifically desirable outcome.



Add formulas

metrics_nested <- 
  metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(H1 = paste0("~ site*position", random))





Collect models

Formulas <-  names(metrics_nested) |> subset(grepl("H1|H0_", names(metrics_nested)))

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Fit models
Models are fitted for each metric using the engine and family specified in the metadata. The fit_model() helper wraps lm, lmer, glmer, and glmmTMB and applies a three-step fallback strategy if a model fails to converge or is singular: first the Date random effect is dropped, then the random slope for position is simplified to a random intercept, and finally the interaction term is removed. This ensures a valid model is returned for every metric while preserving as much complexity as the data will support.
In addition to the main H1 model, several reduced models are fitted for each metric to support partial \[R^2\] decomposition later: models without the Date random effect, without the random slope for position, and without the position fixed effect altogether.



Helper functions

main_formula <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (position|Id) + (1|Date) 
red_formula <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (position|Id)
red_formula2 <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (1|Id)

rhs_same <- function(f1, f2) {
  identical(
    attr(terms(formula(f1, rhs = 1)), "term.labels"),
    attr(terms(formula(f2, rhs = 1)), "term.labels")
  )
}

fit_model <- function(data, formula, engine, family) {
  if(is.null(formula)) return()
  model <- 
  switch(engine,
         "lm" = lm(formula, data = data, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glm" = glm(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "lmer" = lmer(formula, data = data, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glmer" = glmer(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glmmTMB" = glmmTMB(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum"))
         )

did_converge <- 
  performance::check_convergence(model) & !check_singularity(model)
 
  if(!did_converge) {
    if(rhs_same(main_formula, formula)) {
      formula <- formula |> update(. ~ . - (1 | Date))
    } else if (rhs_same(red_formula, formula)) {
      formula <-  formula |> update(. ~ . - (position|Id) + (1|Id))
    } else if (rhs_same(red_formula2, formula)) {
      formula <-  formula |> update(. ~ . - site:position)
    } else return(model)
      
  model <- fit_model(data, formula, engine, family)
  }
  
  model

}





Model fit

metrics_nested <-
  metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(
    H1_model = pmap(list(data, H1, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 model fitting"),
    converged = map_lgl(H1_model, check_convergence),
    singular = map_lgl(H1_model, check_singularity),
    #For R^2:
    H1_fin = map(H1_model, formula),
    H1_no_position = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site:position - position - (position|Id) + (1|Id))),
    H0 = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site*position)),
    H1_no_date = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - (1|Date))),
    H0_no_date = H1_no_date |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site*position)),
    H1_no_slope = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - (position|Id) + (1|Id))),
    H0_no_slope = H1_no_slope |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ .  - site*position)),
    H0_model = pmap(list(data, H0, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 model fitting"),
    H1_no_position_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_position, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no position model fitting"),
    H1_no_date_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_date, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no date model fitting"),
    H0_no_date_model = pmap(list(data, H0_no_date, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 no date model fitting"),
    H1_no_slope_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_slope, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no position slope model fitting"),
    H0_no_slope_model = pmap(list(data, H0_no_slope, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 no position slope model fitting")
    )


After model fitting, all models converged and aren’t singular. This was achieved through a stepwise reduction of model complexity. The two checks below confirm this: all H1 models must have converged (TRUE) and none should be singular (FALSE).



Checks for singularity and convergence

metrics_nested |> pull(converged) |> all() #did all converge


[1] TRUE

metrics_nested |> pull(singular) |> any() #any are singular?

[1] FALSE

title: Comparison of metrics
text:
Extract model results
Several quantities are extracted from every fitted H1 model:

p-values via car::Anova() (Type II/III Wald tests) for the fixed effects position, site, and their interaction.
Model diagnostics via performance::check_model() for visual inspection.
Random-effect standard deviations to quantify between-participant and between-date variability.
Estimated marginal means for the glasses reference level and pairwise contrasts of chest/wrist versus glasses (the two comparisons of primary interest).
Site-level contrasts within each wearing position to flag sites that deviate systematically.
Partial \[R^2\] values (Nakagawa–Schielzeth method) decomposed into contributions from the position fixed effect, the site fixed effect, the random slope for position across participants, the random effect of date, the residual participant intercept, and unexplained residual variance.




Extract model results

sig.level <- 0.05
metrics_nested <-
  metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(
         pvalues = map(H1_model, \(x) Anova(x) |> tidy()),
         diagnostics = map(H1_model, check_model),
         random_effects = map(H1_model,
                              \(x) x |>
                                  tidy() |>
                                         filter(effect == "ran_pars") |>
                                          select(term, group, estimate)
                                          ),
         main_effect = map(H1_model,
                           \(x) x |>
                             emmeans(specs =  ~ 1, at = list(position = "glasses")) |>
                             as.tibble()),
         position_effect = map(H1_model,
                           \(x) x |>
                             emmeans(specs =  ~ position) |>
                             contrast(method = "trt.vs.ctrl") |>
                             as.tibble()),
         site_effect = map(H1_model,
                           \(x) x |>
                             emmeans(specs =  ~ site | position) |>
                             contrast() |>
                             as.tibble()),
           r2_1 = map2(H1_model, H0_model, 
                     \(x,y) r2_nakagawa(x, null_model = y)),
           r2_no_date = map2(H1_no_date_model, H0_no_date_model, 
                     \(x,y) r2_nakagawa(x, null_model = y)),
           r2_no_slope = map2(H1_no_slope_model, H0_no_slope_model, 
                     \(x,y) r2_nakagawa(x, null_model = y)),
           r2_no_position = map2(H1_no_position_model, H0_no_slope_model,
                     \(x,y) r2_nakagawa(x, null_model = y)),
           r2_residual = r2_1 |> map_dbl(\(x) 1 - x$R2_conditional),
           r2_random = r2_1 |> map_dbl(\(x) x$R2_conditional - x$R2_marginal),
           r2_fixed = r2_1 |> map_dbl(\(x) x$R2_marginal),
           r2_position = map2_dbl(r2_1, r2_no_position,
                          \(x, y) x$R2_marginal - y$R2_marginal),
           r2_slope = map2_dbl(r2_1, r2_no_slope, 
                          \(x, y) (x$R2_conditional - x$R2_marginal) - 
                            (y$R2_conditional - y$R2_marginal)),
           r2_date = map2_dbl(r2_1, r2_no_date, 
                          \(x, y) (x$R2_conditional - x$R2_marginal) - 
                            (y$R2_conditional - y$R2_marginal)),
           r2_id = r2_random - r2_slope - r2_date,
           r2_site = r2_fixed - r2_position
         )

text:
Visualize results
Two complementary histograms summarise the distribution of wearing-position errors across all metrics. The first shows absolute errors (ignoring direction), giving a sense of overall magnitude. The second shows signed errors, revealing whether chest and wrist positions tend to over- or underestimate relative to glasses. In both plots, bins corresponding to statistically significant errors are highlighted in the wearing-position color and labelled with the metric name; non-significant errors are shown in grey. Both figures are saved as vector PDFs.



Visualize absolute metric errors

# Helper: recolor strip backgrounds by position after plot build
color_strips <- function(p, fills) {
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  strip_idx <- grep("strip-t", g$layout$name)
  for (i in seq_along(strip_idx)) {
    g$grobs[[strip_idx[i]]]$grobs[[1]]$children[[1]]$gp$fill <- fills[i]
  }
  g
}

normalization_caption <- paste(
  paste0(
    "Brightness-based timing metrics: mean wake duration ",
    mean_wake_duration_label, " (1% = ", mean_wake_one_percent_label, ")."
  ),
  paste0(
    "Darkness-based timing metrics: mean sleep duration ",
    mean_sleep_duration_label, " (1% = ", mean_sleep_one_percent_label, ")."
  ),
  "All other metrics: absolute glasses reference.",
  sep = "\n"
)
combined_bias_caption <- paste(
  "Bin width = 5%; significant errors are highlighted in the position color."
)

fig_abs_error <- 
reduced_df |> 
  select(metric, p_chest:error_wrist) |> 
  pivot_longer(-metric, names_sep = "_", names_to = c("type", "position")) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = value) |> 
  mutate(p = p< 0.05) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = abs(error))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, aes(fill = position)) +
  facet_wrap(~position, labeller = labeller(position = str_to_title)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,1)) +
  # guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(y = "Count (n)", x = "Absolute normalized outcome-level bias (%)") +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines")) +
  gghighlight(p, use_group_by = FALSE,

title: Comparison of metrics - without removing non-wear times
text:
Import
The pre-processed metrics are loaded from a single .RData file produced by the preparation notebook. This object (metrics) is a long-format data frame with one row per participant, date, wearing position, and metric.

#| label: import-metrics
load(here("data/prepared_metrics_nonwear.RData"))


Derive wake and sleep duration denominators
Timing differences are expressed relative to the behavioural interval in which the underlying metric is defined. The sleep interval follows the preparation workflow and extends from diary-recorded sleepprep (when the devices were positioned for the night) to wake. Diary intervals are restricted to participant-dates retained in the prepared metrics, with each interval assigned to its wake date. Mean sleep duration is the grand mean across all retained diary intervals, so each retained night receives equal weight. Mean wake duration is the complement of mean sleep duration to 24 hours. The three darkest-10-hour timing outcomes are classified as darkness-based; all other timing outcomes are classified as brightness-based.



Derive grand-mean wake and sleep durations

#| label: derive-state-duration-denominators
#| filename: Derive grand-mean wake and sleep durations
#| message: false
#| warning: false
analysis_days <-
  metrics |>
  filter(!is.na(Date)) |>
  transmute(
    Id = as.character(Id),
    Date = as.Date(Date)
  ) |>
  distinct()

sleep_intervals <-
  load_data("sleepdiaries") |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "diary_site") |>
  filter(
    !is.na(sleepprep),
    !is.na(wake)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Id = as.character(Id),
    Date = as.Date(wake),
    sleep_duration_seconds = as.numeric(
      difftime(wake, sleepprep, units = "secs")
    )
  ) |>
  semi_join(analysis_days, by = join_by(Id, Date))

invalid_sleep_intervals <-
  sleep_intervals |>
  filter(
    !is.finite(sleep_duration_seconds) |
      sleep_duration_seconds <= 0 |
      sleep_duration_seconds >= 24 * 60 * 60
  )

if (nrow(invalid_sleep_intervals) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "At least one diary-defined sleep interval is outside (0, 24) hours.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

mean_sleep_duration_seconds <- mean(sleep_intervals$sleep_duration_seconds)
mean_wake_duration_seconds <- 24 * 60 * 60 - mean_sleep_duration_seconds

format_duration <- function(seconds) {
  total_minutes <- round(seconds / 60)
  sprintf(
    "%d h %02d min",
    total_minutes %/% 60,
    total_minutes %% 60
  )
}

mean_sleep_duration_label <- format_duration(mean_sleep_duration_seconds)
mean_wake_duration_label <- format_duration(mean_wake_duration_seconds)
mean_sleep_one_percent_label <-
  sprintf("%.1f min", mean_sleep_duration_seconds / 100 / 60)
mean_wake_one_percent_label <-
  sprintf("%.1f min", mean_wake_duration_seconds / 100 / 60)

darkness_timing_metrics <- c(
  "darkest_10h_midpoint",
  "darkest_10h_onset",
  "darkest_10h_offset"
)

timing_normalization_footnote <- paste0(
  "Timing effects and timing-model SDs use the grand mean ",
  "diary-defined wake duration (", mean_wake_duration_label,
  "; 1% = ", mean_wake_one_percent_label,
  ") for brightness-based timing metrics and the grand mean ",
  "diary-defined sleep duration (", mean_sleep_duration_label,
  "; 1% = ", mean_sleep_one_percent_label,
  ") for darkness-based timing metrics. All other metrics use the absolute ",
  "glasses reference on the modelling scale."
)


The resulting grand means are 15 h 45 min of wake and 8 h 15 min of sleep. Consequently, 1% represents 9.4 min for brightness-based timing metrics and 5.0 min for darkness-based timing metrics.

title: Comparison of metrics - without removing non-wear times
text:
Preparing metric table
The raw metrics data frame is restructured for per-metric modelling. Factor levels are set for position, Id, site, and Date (missing dates are replaced with a sentinel value so they don’t drop). The data are then nested so that each row in metrics_nested holds all observations for a single metric.



nest data

#| label: nest-metrics
#| filename: nest data
metrics_nested <-
  metrics |> 
  mutate(Date = replace_na(Date, as_date("2024-09-01")),
         position = factor(position, levels = c("glasses", "chest", "wrist")),
         Id = factor(Id),
         site = factor(site),
         Date = factor(Date)) |> 
  nest(data = -c(metric))


Metadata for each metric (model engine, response transformation, metric type, etc.) is read from an Excel file. The engine column determines which modelling function to use (lm, lmer, glmer, glmmTMB), and the corresponding distributional family is constructed here. The metadata is then joined onto the nested data frame so every metric row knows how it should be modelled.



Load metric information

#| label: load-metric-info
#| filename: Load metric information
metric_info <- read_xlsx(here("data/metric_types.xlsx"))
metric_info <- 
metric_info |> 
  mutate(family = map(engine, \(x) switch(x,
                              "lm" = gaussian(),
                              "lmer" = gaussian(),
                              "glmer" = poisson(),
                              "glmmTMB" = tweedie(link = "log"))),
         family = map2(family, note, 
                       \(x,y) ifelse(is.na(y), return(x), return(poisson()))
                       )
         ) |> 
  select(-note)





Combine metric data and metadata

#| label: join-metric-metadata
#| filename: Combine metric data and metadata
metrics_nested <- 
metrics_nested |> 
  left_join(metric_info, by = join_by(metric == name))



Scaling nighttime metrics
Metrics that capture timing and might cross midnight need to be rescaled in order to work with linear models. The next plot shows the distribution of timing metrics.



show distribution of timing metrics

#| label: fig-timing-distribution
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 15
#| filename: show distribution of timing metrics
#| warning: false
metrics_nested |> 
  filter(metric_type == "timing") |> 
  unnest(data) |> 
    group_by(Id, metric) |> 
  mutate(
    position = fct_relevel(position, c("chest", "glasses", "wrist")),
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=position, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(col = position), height = 0,             
              width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(col = position, fill = position), alpha = 0.5,
               width = 0.1,
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.2)) +
  geom_violinhalf(aes(x = position, y = value,
                   col = position, fill = position), 
              position = position_nudge(x = +0.3),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors) + 
  facet_wrap(~metric, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  guides(col = "none", fill = "none") +
  labs(y = "Scaled and centered metric values",
       x = "Wearing position",
       title = "Raincloud plots of scaled and centered metric results",
       subtitle = scenario_label) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  scale_y_time()

Affected metrics are:

Both show a clear split of the data around midnight. To resolve this, we will shift the datas so that data after 12:00 midday are negative values (i.e., indicate time before midnight).



Transform nighttime timing metrics

#| label: rescale-nighttime-metrics
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 15
#| filename: Transform nighttime timing metrics
metrics_nested <- 
metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(data = map2(data, metric, 
                     \(data, name) {
                       if(name %in% c("darkest_10h_midpoint", "darkest_10h_onset")) {
                         data |> 
                           mutate(value = 
                                    ifelse(value >= (12*60*60), 
                                           value - 24*60*60, 
                                           value)
                                  )
                       } else data
                     }))

title: Comparison of metrics - without removing non-wear times
text:
Prepare modelling
The primary hypothesis (H1) is that wearing position affects a metric, potentially differently across measurement sites (i.e., a site × position interaction). The right-hand side of the formula is assembled here by appending the pre-specified random-effects structure (stored in the random column of metric_info) to the fixed-effects template ~ site*position. A helper then collects all formula column names (H0 and H1 variants) for programmatic iteration.
The table below summarises the modelling specification for every metric: the response variable, any pre-transformation applied, the modelling engine, the distributional family, and the full H1 formula. Confirmatory analyses deliberately omit p-value correction, because a non-significant position effect is the more scientifically desirable outcome.



Add formulas

#| label: add-formulas
#| filename: Add formulas
metrics_nested <- 
  metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(H1 = paste0("~ site*position", random))





Collect models

#| label: collect-formula-names
#| filename: Collect models
Formulas <-  names(metrics_nested) |> subset(grepl("H1|H0_", names(metrics_nested)))



#| label: tbl-model-specs
#| echo: false
metrics_nested |> 
  select(-data, -random) |>
  arrange(metric_type, metric_family, metric) |> 
  mutate(family = map(family, 1),
         rowname = seq_along(1:length(metric))) |> 
  group_by(metric_type) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label_with(fn = \(x) x |> str_to_title() |> str_replace_all("_", " ")) |> 
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |> 
  sub_values(values = "NULL", replacement = "") |> 
  fmt(c(metric, pre.transformed, response), fns = \(x) x |> str_to_title() |>  str_replace_all("_", " ")) |> 
  sub_values(values = "MDER", replacement = "MDER") |> 
  tab_header("Metric model specifications",
             subtitle = paste(
               "Hypothesis: wearing position affects metric result within sites.",
               scenario_label
             )) |>
  tab_footnote("Confirmatory analysis will use no p-value correction, as a non-significant difference result is the more desired result") |> 
  tab_footnote("These are the models used for the analysis per metric. H1 is tested with car::Anova to inspect the significant portions", locations = cells_column_labels(Formulas)) |> 
  cols_width(
    Formulas ~ px(200),
    c(metric, pre.transformed, response) ~ px(125),
    everything() ~ px(80))

title: Comparison of metrics - without removing non-wear times
text:
Fit models
Models are fitted for each metric using the engine and family specified in the metadata. The fit_model() helper wraps lm, lmer, glmer, and glmmTMB and applies a three-step fallback strategy if a model fails to converge or is singular: first the Date random effect is dropped, then the random slope for position is simplified to a random intercept, and finally the interaction term is removed. This ensures a valid model is returned for every metric while preserving as much complexity as the data will support.
In addition to the main H1 model, several reduced models are fitted for each metric to support partial \[R^2\] decomposition later: models without the Date random effect, without the random slope for position, and without the position fixed effect altogether.



Helper functions

#| label: fit-model-helpers
#| filename: Helper functions
main_formula <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (position|Id) + (1|Date) 
red_formula <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (position|Id)
red_formula2 <- value ~ site*position + site + position + (1|Id)

rhs_same <- function(f1, f2) {
  identical(
    attr(terms(formula(f1, rhs = 1)), "term.labels"),
    attr(terms(formula(f2, rhs = 1)), "term.labels")
  )
}

fit_model <- function(data, formula, engine, family) {
  if(is.null(formula)) return()
  model <- 
  switch(engine,
         "lm" = lm(formula, data = data, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glm" = glm(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "lmer" = lmer(formula, data = data, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glmer" = glmer(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum")),
         "glmmTMB" = glmmTMB(formula, data = data, family = family, contrasts = list(site = "contr.sum"))
         )

did_converge <- 
  performance::check_convergence(model) & !check_singularity(model)
 
  if(!did_converge) {
    if(rhs_same(main_formula, formula)) {
      formula <- formula |> update(. ~ . - (1 | Date))
    } else if (rhs_same(red_formula, formula)) {
      formula <-  formula |> update(. ~ . - (position|Id) + (1|Id))
    } else if (rhs_same(red_formula2, formula)) {
      formula <-  formula |> update(. ~ . - site:position)
    } else return(model)
      
  model <- fit_model(data, formula, engine, family)
  }
  
  model

}





Model fit

#| label: fit-all-models
#| filename: Model fit
#| message: false
#| warning: false
metrics_nested <-
  metrics_nested |> 
  mutate(
    H1_model = pmap(list(data, H1, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 model fitting"),
    converged = map_lgl(H1_model, check_convergence),
    singular = map_lgl(H1_model, check_singularity),
    #For R^2:
    H1_fin = map(H1_model, formula),
    H1_no_position = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site:position - position - (position|Id) + (1|Id))),
    H0 = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site*position)),
    H1_no_date = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - (1|Date))),
    H0_no_date = H1_no_date |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - site*position)),
    H1_no_slope = H1_fin |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ . - (position|Id) + (1|Id))),
    H0_no_slope = H1_no_slope |> map(\(x) update(x, . ~ .  - site*position)),
    H0_model = pmap(list(data, H0, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 model fitting"),
    H1_no_position_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_position, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no position model fitting"),
    H1_no_date_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_date, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no date model fitting"),
    H0_no_date_model = pmap(list(data, H0_no_date, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 no date model fitting"),
    H1_no_slope_model = pmap(list(data, H1_no_slope, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H1 no position slope model fitting"),
    H0_no_slope_model = pmap(list(data, H0_no_slope, engine, family), fit_model, .progress = "H0 no position slope model fitting")
    )
